answers.children: Afghan Hounds are moderately good with children when raised together. Their large size, independent nature and limited patience with rough play can lead to standoffish behaviour around boisterous youngsters, while their history as agile sighthounds means they prefer calm interaction over constant activity. The dignified temperament often results in gentle affection on the hound’s own terms rather than eager engagement. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 5/10)
answers.other-pets: Afghan Hounds do not always get along with other pets. Strong prey drive from their origins hunting deer and wolves in Afghanistan makes them likely to chase smaller animals, and their aloof temperament can create standoffish or tense relations especially with same-sex dogs or unfamiliar pets.
answers.exercise: Afghan Hounds need at least an hour of exercise daily. Bred for sight hunting across rugged Afghan terrain, they require safe open space to run at full speed and excel at lure coursing; without it their athletic build leads to boredom expressed through destructive chewing or restlessness indoors.
answers.shedding: Yes, Afghan Hounds shed moderately year-round. Their long silky coat with flowing feathering tangles easily and spreads fine hair across furniture and floors, while the protective coat developed for extreme Afghan temperatures demands regular removal of loose undercoat to limit indoor debris.
answers.hypoallergenic: The Afghan Hound has a long silky coat that sheds moderately and releases hair around the home; the flowing locks also mat easily without daily attention. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic and the Afghan Hound is not among those usually suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: Afghan Hounds are not easy to train. Their independent thinking developed for hunting large game without constant human direction, combined with an aloof and dignified temperament, reduces biddability so they often ignore commands in favour of following their own instincts.
answers.lifespan: Afghan Hounds live 12-15 years. The breed’s athletic and agile build, honed over centuries for chasing prey on harsh mountainous ground, supports reasonable health robustness, yet its large frame and sensitivity to stress mean owners must provide consistent exercise and calm routines to help reach the upper end of that range.
answers.size: Adult Afghan Hounds weigh 50-60 lb and stand 25-27 in tall. The elegant, lean proportions and long silky coat create a striking yet surprisingly substantial presence in the home, where their height allows them to rest their head easily on counters or furniture while their agility lets them navigate tight spaces gracefully.
answers.barking: Afghan Hounds do not bark a lot. Their history as independent sighthounds that tracked game by sight across vast landscapes has left them generally quiet and reserved, so they tend to stay silent unless something truly captures their attention, reflecting their dignified and aloof character.
answers.apartment: Afghan Hounds can live in an apartment only with considerable effort. Their need for daily running in secure open areas, high grooming demands from the long silky coat, and tendency to become bored and destructive when under-exercised outweigh any indoor settling ability despite their calm, dignified temperament at rest.
answers.first-time: Afghan Hounds are not a good first dog. The combination of high grooming demands from their unique flowing coat, strong independent streak that resists training, and sensitivity to stress requires experienced handling to manage their aloof nature and prevent frustration for novice owners.
